hints: Focus on where strontium sits in Group 2, below magnesium and calcium but above barium, as almost all properties follow a trend down the group.
Remember that hydroxides get more soluble down the group, sulfates get less soluble, and nitrates get more thermally stable down the group.
Consider how easily atoms lose electrons down the group as atomic size increases and ionisation energy falls, and link this to reducing strength.
walkthrough:
**Place the elements in Group 2**

Magnesium is at the top, then calcium, then strontium, then barium at the bottom. Most Group 2 trends are smooth down the group, so we can compare Sr with Mg, Ca and Ba.

Order down group: $\text{Mg} > \text{Ca} > \text{Sr} > \text{Ba}$ (top to bottom)

**Recall the solubility and stability trends**

Hydroxides become more soluble down the group. Sulfates become less soluble down the group. Nitrates and carbonates become more thermally stable down the group because the larger cation polarises the anion less.

Nitrate decomposition: $$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Apply the trends to the statements**

Strontium hydroxide must be less soluble than barium hydroxide below it. Strontium sulfate must be less soluble than magnesium sulfate above it. Strontium nitrate must be more stable than calcium nitrate above it.

So the first three comparisons are the wrong way round.

**Check reducing power**

Down the group, atoms get larger and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. First and second ionisation energies fall, so electrons are lost more easily.

$$\text{Sr} \rightarrow \text{Sr}^{2+} + 2e^-$$

Strontium loses electrons more readily than magnesium, so it is oxidised more easily and is the stronger reducing agent. This is the correct statement.

options.A: Incorrect. Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group, so $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is more soluble than $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$. This option reverses the trend.
options.B: Incorrect. Group 2 sulfates become less soluble down the group, so $\text{MgSO}_4$ is very soluble while $\text{SrSO}_4$ is sparingly soluble. This option reverses the trend.
options.C: Incorrect. Group 2 nitrates become more thermally stable down the group because the larger $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ ion distorts the nitrate ion less than the smaller $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ ion. So strontium nitrate has higher, not lower, thermal stability than calcium nitrate.
options.D: Correct. Reactivity and reducing power increase down Group 2. Strontium is larger than magnesium with lower ionisation energies, so it loses its two outer electrons more easily and acts as a stronger reducing agent.
